b: On May 19 the sky went black at midday across New England. In Hartford, legislators feared Judgment Day; Abraham Davenport told them to bring candles and keep working.

t: First witch hanging in the colonies
b: Alse Young was hanged in Hartford in 1647, the first recorded execution for witchcraft in the American colonies.
Legend says Connecticut's royal charter was snatched in a darkened room and hidden in a hollow oak to keep it from Governor Andros.
Booming and rumbling from under the hills. The Wangunk called the place Machimoodus, 'place of noises'; colonists blamed witches and a buried giant gem.
A silent wanderer in a 60-pound leather suit walked a 365-mile loop through Connecticut and New York every 34 days. He died in 1889; who he was is still debated.
A hill village abandoned by about 1900. Later writers spun a 'curse' of madness and misfortune around it; locals dispute the story.
Stone chambers and a double stone circle in Groton's woods. Colonial root cellars, or something much older? Their age is still argued.
During a tuberculosis outbreak, villagers exhumed 19-year-old Mercy Brown, burned her heart, and gave the ashes to her dying brother.
A round stone tower on arches. A colonial windmill from around 1670, or built by Norse voyagers centuries earlier? Mortar dating points colonial.
A boulder in the Taunton River covered in carvings, first sketched in 1680. Readers have seen Norse, Phoenician, Portuguese and Native writing in it.
Accusations that began with 'afflicted' girls led to 19 hangings, and one man pressed to death under stones.
In August, dozens of townspeople reported a huge serpent in the harbor. Boston's Linnean Society took sworn statements from witnesses.
Engraver William Mumler sold portraits with ghostly relatives behind the sitters. Tried for fraud in New York in 1869, he was acquitted.
Stone chambers and standing stones billed as 'America's Stonehenge'. A 19th-century farm, or an ancient calendar site?
Crowds came to a Vermont farmhouse where William and Horatio Eddy were said to summon full-form spirits. Henry Olcott met Helena Blavatsky there.
A county sheriff reported a huge serpent in the lake in 1883, and P. T. Barnum later offered a reward for its hide. Sightings of 'Champ' continue.
The New York Sun ran a series claiming an astronomer had seen bat-winged people and unicorns on the Moon. Readers believed it for weeks.
Well diggers 'found' a 10-foot stone man on a farm. It was a carved hoax, but crowds paid to see it, and P. T. Barnum made his own copy.
Two sisters in a farmhouse claimed knocking sounds answered their questions. It launched Spiritualism; forty years later one sister said they had faked it.
Tesla's 187-foot tower on Long Island, meant to send messages and power without wires. Funding ran out, and it was torn down in 1917.
In January, people across the Delaware Valley reported hoofprints in snow and a winged creature; some schools and mills closed. The legend traces to 1735.
A 1950s legend says the USS Eldridge was made invisible at the Navy Yard in 1943. The Navy says it never happened.
A small stone with unknown letters was reported from inside the giant Grave Creek Mound. Its script has been called Celtic, Phoenician and fake.
An 1885 pamphlet said three ciphers lead to buried gold. One was solved using the Declaration of Independence; two remain unsolved.
Returning in 1590, John White found the colony gone and 'CROATOAN' carved on a post. The colonists were never found.
Glowing orbs seen bobbing above the ridge. A 1913 government report blamed train lights; sightings continued anyway.
The Bell family reported a spirit that talked, slapped and tormented them for years. Local tradition ties it to John Bell's death in 1820.
A Smithsonian dig in a burial mound turned up a stone with letters later read as Paleo-Hebrew. Most scholars consider it a forgery.
In March, flakes of what looked like meat fell from a clear sky onto a farm. Explanations ranged from vomiting buzzards to a kind of algae.
A quarter-mile earthen snake on an Ohio ridge, its head aligned with the summer solstice sunset. Who built it, and when, is still debated.
A city of earthen pyramids near St. Louis that peaked around 1100 with perhaps 10,000 to 40,000 people, then emptied.
Residents reported a prowler spraying sweet-smelling gas into homes. Police later called it mass hysteria.
Slate tablets with zodiac signs and a strange script, 'found' in a mound. Exposed as a prank, but argued over for decades.
A farmer dug up a stone carved with runes describing Norse explorers in 1362. Most scholars call it a modern fake; some still defend it.
A newspaper item said an airship hit a windmill and its pilot, 'not an inhabitant of this world', was buried in town. Most historians call it a hoax.
Unexplained lights east of Marfa. A cowboy named Robert Ellison is said to have first reported them in 1883.
The Army announced it had recovered a 'flying disc', then said it was a weather balloon. Decades later it was tied to the secret Project Mogul.
In his mountain lab, Tesla recorded regular signals he thought might come from another planet. Likely natural radio, or Marconi's tests.
Jacob Waltz died in 1891 talking of a rich gold mine in the mountains. Searchers have hunted it, and some have died, ever since.
In November, Sacramento residents reported a lighted airship over the city. Sightings spread across the country into 1897.
Anti-aircraft guns fired more than 1,400 shells into the night sky after reports of enemy planes. No aircraft were ever found.
A pilot reported nine shiny objects skipping past Mount Rainier in June. Newspapers coined the phrase 'flying saucer'.
Five Navy bombers left on a training flight in December and vanished; a rescue plane was lost too. The Bermuda Triangle legend grew from it.
A 100-pound Latvian immigrant quarried and moved tons of coral rock alone, at night. He said he knew the secrets of the pyramids.
A teenager found a sunken patch under an oak in 1795; diggers hit log platforms every few feet down. Two centuries of treasure hunts followed.
Found adrift and seaworthy in December, cargo intact, and no one aboard. The crew was never seen again.
A relief boat found the lighthouse empty in December. All three keepers were gone; one set of oilskins hung on its peg.

t: St. Columba and the River Ness beast
b: A biography written around 700 tells how Columba drove a 'water beast' away from a swimmer in the River Ness: the oldest Loch Ness monster story.
Two cousins photographed 'fairies' by a stream. Arthur Conan Doyle believed them; in 1983 they admitted the fairies were paper cutouts.
Reports of a leaping figure with claws and fiery eyes spread from 1837. The Lord Mayor read a complaint about him aloud in 1838.
Richard Carrington watched a solar flare from his observatory. Within days, auroras lit skies near the tropics and telegraph wires sparked.
After a February snowfall, hoof-like tracks ran for miles across south Devon, over walls and rooftops, people said.
Medieval chroniclers told of a green-skinned boy and girl found by the wolf pits, speaking an unknown language.
Begun about 3000 BC; the big sarsens went up around 2500 BC. Aligned to midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset.
A passage tomb older than the pyramids. At winter solstice dawn, a beam of sunlight runs down the passage and lights the inner chamber.
Fifteen villagers said they saw silent, glowing figures at the church gable on a rainy August evening.
More than 3,000 standing stones in long rows, set up mostly between about 4500 and 3300 BC.
A wolf-like animal was blamed for dozens of deadly attacks between 1764 and 1767. King Louis XV sent his own hunters.
Bernadette Soubirous, 14, reported eighteen visions of a lady in the Massabielle grotto.
Abbe Sauniere arrived in 1885 and later spent lavishly. Rumors of a hidden treasure or secret grew into a 20th-century legend.
In July a woman began dancing in the street and couldn't stop. Within weeks dozens had joined; officials hired musicians to dance it out.
A broadsheet described black globes racing through the sunrise sky over Basel in the summer of 1566.
A broadsheet reported crosses, globes and tubes battling in the dawn sky on April 14. Its woodcut is a UFO-lore favorite.
A teenage boy appeared in the square with a letter, saying he'd spent his life in a dark cell. Rumor made him a hidden prince.
Old town records note that 130 children left Hamelin on June 26, 1284. Plague, a crusade, or settlers heading east? No one knows.
A linen cloth bearing a man's faint image, first recorded in Lirey, France, in the 1350s. Radiocarbon tests in 1988 dated it to the Middle Ages.
A book in an unknown script, full of strange plants and bathing figures, bought by Wilfrid Voynich in 1912. Its vellum dates to the early 1400s. No one has read it.
Sponge divers pulled a corroded bronze lump from an ancient wreck. Inside was a geared calculator for predicting eclipses, about 2,000 years old.
An Ottoman admiral's world map, found in Topkapi Palace in 1929. Some say it shows Antarctica's coast; mainstream scholars disagree.
Carved stone pillars on a hilltop, raised about 11,500 years ago: before writing, pottery or the wheel.
A city cut deep into soft rock, with air shafts, wells, stables and rolling stone doors. Big enough to shelter thousands; rediscovered in 1963.
A Roman temple platform resting on stones of around 800 tons each. Blocks over 1,000 tons still lie in the nearby quarry.
A clay jar holding a copper cylinder and an iron rod, found in 1936. An ancient battery, or a holder for sacred scrolls?
Built around 2560 BC from about 2.3 million blocks. It was the tallest structure on Earth for over 3,800 years.
A wooden bird model found in a tomb in 1898. Fringe writers call it a glider; Egyptologists see a toy or a weather vane.
Temple reliefs show a lotus-and-snake shape some call an ancient light bulb. Egyptologists read it as a creation myth.
A 7-meter iron pillar about 1,600 years old that has barely rusted. Metallurgists credit its high phosphorus content.
An explosion over Siberia flattened about 2,000 square km of forest. No crater was found; most think a meteor burst in the air.

t: Tambora and the year without a summer
b: The largest eruption in recorded history. The next year, snow fell in New England in June and harvests failed across Europe.
Stories told of a freighter found with its whole crew dead, faces frozen in fear, before it burned and sank. No record of the ship has been found.
Giant animals and lines scraped into the desert between about 500 BC and 500 AD, best seen from the air.
Inca walls of huge stone blocks fitted so tightly that a knife blade won't slip between them.
Precisely cut stone blocks with interlocking joints, part of the Tiwanaku complex. They fuel endless theories.
Giant basalt heads carved about 3,000 years ago and moved many miles without wheels or draft animals.
Nearly 1,000 stone figures. Islanders said the moai 'walked' to their platforms; experiments show they can be rocked upright along a road.
